opus-5.5.text:
I think what struck me most was how simple the idea was, and yet how surprising the result felt. At that time I was an undergrad in the Yao Class at Tsinghua, and in Professor Li Jian's course he showed this demonstration where you embed words and images into a shared vector space. You could do things like take the image of something, subtract one concept, add another word, and the nearest neighbor would come back as a sensible image. It's the old "king minus man plus woman equals queen" trick, but extended across modalities.

What hit me wasn't really the engineering. It was the realization that meaning could be captured by geometry, that just by training on lots of data with a fairly simple objective, the model would discover structure that we never explicitly told it about. Language and vision, two very different kinds of signals, somehow lined up in the same space. That felt almost philosophical to me: maybe a lot of what we call understanding is just learning the right representation.

Before that, I was more into theory, algorithms, the kind of problems where you have a clean proof. That demo was one of the first moments when I felt deep learning wasn't just curve fitting. There was something general going on. It made me curious about language in particular, because language seemed like the place where all these concepts get compressed and connected. Looking back, that curiosity is part of what pushed me toward NLP, and later toward language agents.

fable-5.1.text:
What really struck me was that it didn't feel like a party trick. Li Jian showed this example where you take the vector for a word and then you look at what image embeddings land near it, and the correspondences were surprisingly reasonable. Not perfect, but reasonable in a way that made you pause.

Up until that point, I think I'd mostly thought of these things as separate problems. Language is one domain, vision is another, and each has its own tooling and its own intuitions. What that demo suggested, almost casually, was that meaning might live in a shared geometric space, and that words and pictures were just two different projections of it. That's a very simple idea once you say it out loud, but seeing it actually work on real data is different from reading about it.

The other thing I remember is how little machinery was involved. It wasn't some enormous system. It was a fairly small model, trained with a fairly simple objective, and the structure just emerged. That stuck with me for a long time, this sense that if you set up the right representation and the right learning signal, a lot of the interesting behavior comes for free. I think a lot of what I've been drawn to since, agents, language models interacting with environments, traces back to that feeling that the representation does most of the work if you let it.

And honestly, part of it was just that it was fun. It made the field feel alive rather than like a set of fixed tools you memorize. That matters a lot when you're a student trying to decide what to spend your years on.
